transcript:
Meeting header:
Date: 2026-05-20
Start: 10:00 UTC
Duration: ~45 minutes
Attendees: Aisha Patel (Redwood AE), Diego Ruiz (Redwood SE), Maya Singh (Quantaco AI - Head of Infra), Jordan Lee (Quantaco ML Eng), Samir Rao (Quantaco CTO)

Summary:
Quick cost/unit economics sync for the POC. Reviewed current benchmark numbers (tokens/sec/$), discussed caching and batching tradeoffs, clarified host vs dedicated cost model, agreed on follow-up benchmarks and artifacts to share.

Topics:
- Current cost baseline (hosted)
- Caching (prefix/KV) observed savings
- Batching parameters and latency tradeoffs
- Quantization options and throughput impact
- Next steps: benchmarks and traffic traces

Transcript:
[00:00] Aisha: hey everyone thanks for joining, we wanted to go over the cost econ numbers you shared last week and talk about next steps on bench marking, um so diego and i will walk through the numbers then open for q.
[00:18] Maya: awesome, thanks aisha. we ran the script you provided, couple of notes - latency looked fine but cost/per token seemed higher than expected on the hosted endpoints.
[00:30] Diego: ok good, so quick primer — the hosted profile uses mixed-precision fp16 kernels by default, and we do prefix caching where we can. the numbers you saw probably include cold cache runs. can you remind us of your typical prompt shapes and reuse?
[00:47] Jordan: yeah most requests are multi-turn chat about 150 tokens total, and we have a lot of repeated system prompts + product description prefixes - i'd estimate prefix reuse ~45% across sessions.
[01:01] Samir: we also sometimes do batch scoring for ranking flows - bursts of 20-50 short inputs (20-40 tokens) at a time.
[01:12] Diego: perfect, that helps. ok so the baseline you shared showed ~0.9 tokens/sec/$ on hosted for the 13B model with default batching. when we enable prefix/KV cache and bump batching to 32 we see tokens/sec/$ jump to ~2.6 in our internal sims, but latency tail can increase for individual requests if you wait to fill a batch.
[01:32] Maya: when you say tokens/sec/$ is that measured at 95th latency or avg? because our concern is both cost and 95th latency for interactive features.
[01:41] Diego: good point — that tokens/sec/$ is aggregate throughput normalized to cost, so it's more of a cost-efficiency metric over time (avg throughput). for 95th latency we saw median ~120ms per response for single-turns on dedicated nodes and 95th ~380ms with batching of 32 on the same hardware.
[01:57] Jordan: so there's a clear tradeoff: if we prioritize low p95 we lose some cost efficiency. is there a middle ground?
[02:04] Aisha: yea, we recommend hybrid policy — route critical interactive traffic to low-latency dedicated pools and batchable background scoring to shared/burst capacity. that keeps user-facing p95 low while capturing batching econ for non-latency-sensitive workloads.
[02:18] Samir: curious about caching numbers — you said prefix reuse can give big wins. do you have a real example from your internal POC?
[02:26] Diego: yes, in your traffic with ~45% prefix reuse, our sample runs show token savings of ~28-35% because repeated tokens are served from KV cache and don't re-run the full forward pass. that translates directly into tokens/sec/$ improvement since fewer args need compute.
[02:41] Maya: is that savings sensitive to sequence length? our average session is 150 tokens but some conversations grow to 600 tokens.
[02:48] Diego: longer sequences make caching slightly less effective for early tokens but the KV cache still helps a lot for repeated prefixes. the hit rate matters more than total length - if the early 100 tokens are identical across users you still save heavily.
[02:59] Jordan: what about quantization? we tried int8 and saw weird quality drop on some prompts.
[03:05] Diego: right — quantization is a spectrum. int8 can yield ~1.4-1.7x throughput improvements and cost drops but may impact hallucination/quality for certain models. our recommendation: run a small eval suite on your most-critical prompts (we can run that) and consider mixed-precision quant or per-layer quant profiles.
[03:21] Samir: and hardware differences, like A100 vs H100 — does that change the tokens/sec/$ story?
[03:27] Diego: yes, H100s have better kernel density for large batches so batching gains are higher on H100; however their hourly cost is also higher. we model tokens/sec/$ per hardware type — often a dedicated H100 pool for high-throughput batch jobs plus hosted rtx-like instances for interactive is a good combo.
[03:42] Maya: can you explain how the billing works for dedicated pools versus hosted, especially for idle time and burst?
[03:48] Aisha: sure — hosted is pure usage-based: you pay per token/second consumed. Dedicated is reserved GPU capacity with a monthly commit; you pay the reserved price even if underutilized, but you get better latency SLOs and lower per-token marginal cost when fully utilized. we offer burst credits to let you exceed committed capacity temporarily.
[04:06] Jordan: ok that makes sense. what's your recommended commit level for our 10k tokens/day profile?
[04:11] Diego: for 10k tokens/day that's relatively low — likely not worth a dedicated pool unless you plan to scale to hundreds of millions tokens/day. Instead, run hosted with aggressive caching + batching for background jobs. if you project 5-10x growth in 3 months then switch to a small dedicated pool.
[04:25] Maya: do you have a simple projection we can use to show when dedicated becomes cost-effective?
[04:29] Aisha: yes we'll share a model — basically a breakeven chart: x-axis traffic, y-axis cost per token, factoring in prefix hit-rate. diego will run a run with your real traces and produce that projection.
[04:39] Samir: another ask — can you instrument tokens/sec/$ by route/model in a way we can plug into our dashboards?
[04:45] Diego: yes, our console exposes per-route cost and latency breakdowns and we can grant read-only tokens for your observability team; we can also produce a csv export for your internal analysis.
[04:56] Jordan: one more operational question — how does caching work for multi-tenant hosted? is there any risk of cross-tenant leakage?
[05:03] Diego: good callout — caches are tenant-isolated; KV caches are logically scoped to customer and model. no cross-tenant leakage. for private deployments we let customers control cache retention policies.
[05:15] Maya: about the benchmark runs you mentioned earlier, what variants should we run? we can start with our baseline and then run with cache/batch/quant combinations.
[05:22] Diego: exactly — baseline (no cache, batch=1, fp16), cache on (default cache policy), batching sweep (1,8,16,32), quant profiles (fp16, int8, mixed). we'll capture median and 95th latencies and tokens/sec/$ for each.
[05:35] Aisha: timeline check — diego can run the benchmark and we can reconvene next week to review. deeb?
[05:41] Diego: yep i'll start today, i'll use the sample traces maya provides and produce a sheet with results and breakeven projections.
[05:47] Maya: i'll export the trace and share it in the slack thread by monday.
[05:51] Samir: ok good, once we have the projection we'll show to finance and prioritize whether we move to dedicated.
[05:58] Aisha: any risks we missed? compliance or encryption concerns tied to caching?
[06:03] Diego: caches respect customer encryption at rest and keys are managed via KMS for private deployments; for hosted we have server-side encryption and audit logs. security doc will be in the packet aisha sends.
[06:14] Jordan: thanks, that addresses a lot.
[06:17] Aisha: cool, quick recap of next steps and action items — diego to run benchmarks, aisha to send pricing and security packet, maya to share traces, schedule deep-dive demo for caching next week.
[06:30] Maya: thanks all.
[06:32] Samir: thanks, talk next week.

End of transcript.
